title: Add design doc for Signed Podman Machine OS images

comments.body: LGTM, couple of nitty questions around clarification; otherwise, this is excellent that we are doing this.  tyvm!

@mtrmac Thanks for the review! Hopefully what I'm saying makes sense, but, let me know if I've misunderstood or I'm missing something - I'm trying to understand the complexity here, which I may have initially underestimated.

To re-word this into a hopefully more specific proposal / chain of thought:

> The way I think about the starting point is “a signature is a claim that $something is true; A. what exactly is the property we are claiming, and then B. is our implementation achieving that at a high enough level of confidence?”.
>
> And for A., I think the intuitive goal to aim for is “the user gets exactly the image they asked for [or things fail and the user gets nothing]”. I.e. users who ask for podman-machine-os:6.2 get podman-machine-os:6.2.

- So, we have software creating a signature as :6.2. How is the software confident that it is signing a legitimate object as :6.2?
  - “The `podman-machine-os` repo contains a tag for 6.2.X, that tag refers to a merged commit on the 6.2 branch (or on the main branch), and the repo has branch protection set up so that merges require N approvals, and adding tags is also locked down $that way”. Is that the rule? (I’m very unsure.)
  - Is it sufficient? Up to us.
     - I think it well might be; we should protect against individual mistakes but we shouldn’t over-complicate things.
     - I don’t think GitHub allows requiring multiple approvals to create a tag. We probably should have immutable tags, at least. _Maybe_ we require the tagged commit to have specific contents signaling the intent for it to be tagged as 6.2.X?
 
---

For B.

> And then it is fine to say “we trust that the workflow file only signs images that were built by our CI, and we trust that the workflow file will create a signature for v6.2 that really corresponds some version that humans decided to be a v6.2 image (and designated using some mechanism)” — because we designed the workflow file that way, and because we keep reviewing the workflow file that way.
> 
> (We should have a discussion about the details here, maybe imposing a stricter review requirements and louder change notifications on the workflow and its dependencies, up to and possibly including moving the workflow and the related secrets, if any, to a separate, much more locked down, repo.)

My hypothetical starting point here is “we have a separate repo that is very locked down; and within that repo a workflow that does the signing. That repo implements our logic for what is allowed to be signed as :6.2. The OIDC token issued for that workflow, and the Fulcio certificate, identify the workflow enough that we can define a `policy.json` rule requiring that the signature came form this workflow”.
- The repo/workflow must not be _totally_ immutable: environments and CLIs change, and we need to be able to change it without the `policy.json` reference to it breaking.
- How does the workflow get triggered and how does it know what signature it was asked to create? That would probably be easier within the same repo, we could trigger on tag creation.
- It doesn’t _have_ to be a separate repo. Maybe just a separate more locked-down branch in the `podman-machine-os` repo. (It probably should not follow the default branch layout of the repo, because “how things are signed” is independent of Podman versioning.)
- Maybe we don’t even need it “more locked-down” than the rest of the repo. The important thing is that we are confident enough it will not be maliciously modified, that changes to it will get noticed, and that we can identify it in the OIDC token / Fulcio certificate.

---

Another thing: The signing operations should produce an audit log — some kind of long-term (not disappearing after N months); and, if at all possible, immutable, record — of everything that was ever signed. (Maybe an add-only S3 bucket??? No idea.)

(Already Fulcio is reportedly creating a transparency log for issued certificates, and all signatures are uploaded to Rekor. But that would also include the hypothetical malicious signatures, so we should have a separate log of what we _intended_ to sign, to be able to detect any completely unexpected signatures.)

> * So, we have software creating a signature as :6.2. How is the software confident that it is signing a legitimate object as :6.2?
>   
>   * “The `podman-machine-os` repo contains a tag for 6.2.X, that tag refers to a merged commit on the 6.2 branch (or on the main branch), and the repo has branch protection set up so that merges require N approvals, and adding tags is also locked down $that way”. Is that the rule? (I’m very unsure.)

This is fine for identifying a _commit_, but not for identifying the binary artifact. IOW “build an OS image; then trigger a super-secure signing workflow” is at most as as strong as the “build OS image step” — actually _weaker_ because the signing workflow has no way to pair the commit with the OS image binary.

So that implies for B., the build itself needs to be driven by the secure workflow. Either we have a trusted “build+sign” workflow (in the previously-suggested separate repo/branch) that is given a target tag/commit, validates it, triggers an “ordinary” build for that commit (however “a build” is defined in the `podman-machine-os` repo as of the target commit), and signs the outcome; or we give up on the separation, and just have a “build an OS image + sign” workflow in the primary `podman-machine-os` repo, and _all of them_ are allowed to create signatures.

I think separating the “determine commit; trigger build; sign the outcome” part from the “build an image from commit” part could be valuable, because we could lock down the top-level+signing part without slowing down development of the the whole repo, but I’m not at all sure it is practical.

> “The podman-machine-os repo contains a tag for 6.2.X, that tag refers to a merged commit on the 6.2 branch (or on the main branch), and the repo has branch protection set up so that merges require N approvals, and adding tags is also locked down $that way”. Is that the rule? (I’m very unsure.)

It not fully configured that way today but I think we really need to configure "environments" and there we can require approvals.

https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/deployments-and-environments#deployment-branches-and-tags

> I don’t think GitHub allows requiring multiple approvals to create a tag. We probably should have immutable tags, at least. Maybe we require the tagged commit to have specific contents signaling the intent for it to be tagged as 6.2.X?

We have immutable releases already setup there. As for preventing tag pushes nor from a branch I am not sure if github allows that directly but with the environments mentioned above we can prevent the CI from triggering on it I think.

Overall I am not sure how well this all works together but I think the ability to lock the workflows down tightly exists. Ultimately if you are an org/repo admin you can disable all protection settings so this can never prevent full account takeover compromises but if somebody just has my ssh key to push to the repo they could not bypass that so it helps a bit.

I don't know if this exists but if we want to protect against the single maintainer compromise I suppose we would need multiple signatures from multiple people? Like maintainer A and B must have signed this and they store those keys locally but then we loose the automated aspect again so that is not the direction we like to go here I think.

> I don't know if this exists but if we want to protect against the single maintainer compromise I suppose we would need multiple signatures from multiple people? Like maintainer A and B must have signed this and they store those keys locally but then we loose the automated aspect again so that is not the direction we like to go here I think.

If we trust GitHub to issue correct OIDC tokens for the signing workflow, we trust GitHub period — so I think we could check whether the commit comes from a PR with 2 GitHub PR approvals, and that would be ~equivalent. Or “only” document that the repo should have 2 approvals, and assume that in the workflow, without checking the specific commit.

Same for “does the commit come from the intended branch”, we can check that ourselves in code, or we can trust GitHub configuration.

I’d _slightly_ prefer the script enforcing policy, because it is visible and it isn’t so easy to disable/override (like we do for merging private branches) without forgetting to re-enable, but that’s not a hard opinion.

> I’d slightly prefer the script enforcing policy, because it is visible and it isn’t so easy to disable/override (like we do for merging private branches) without forgetting to re-enable, but that’s not a hard opinion.

Well I guess we need both then, a script does not help if somebody can push a commit/tag they can remove the check in the script as part of a commit they tagged. Now I agree that such malicious action would be more visible as part of the git history not some private setting that can be turned-off at any time.

That’s why I think the signing workflow would be better separate from, and more protected than, the full `podman-machine-os` repo (and why the very start of my comments was about “did we use version 6.1.10 to sign 6.1.10”, although I no longer think that kind of matching is preferable).

Okay, so the way we have it currently set up is that the build (and in this proposal, build+sign) step are run in the same workflow. They are separate jobs in the workflow, but since they are in the same workflow, we pretty much guarantee that the signed image is the one we built. This build+sign+release workflow is triggered off a tag of the version bump commit, so the flow would look something like this:
 
1. Open PR to bump version on a branch
2. Maintainers /approve and merge the pr
3. Maintainer with push access tags the version bump commit

I think this in itself is secure enough since a maintainer has to do two steps manually, verify the PR and actually tag. The workflow that runs is the version of the workflow that exists on the branch that the tag is cut off of, and the it's configured to be triggered off tags. I think there's enough security there too that we don't have to worry about the workflow being maliciously edited - we have branch protection that prevents pushes and require pull requests for edits. The way our GitHub is set up already checks for these things; the only way this would fail is if a account with admin privs was compromised, but at that point, they could force push anything. However, it's pretty trivial to add a few lines of bash in our workflow that checks branch and commit; I'm not opposed to adding that

I think I'd prefer to keep everything in the podman-machine-os repo. If this automation lived somewhere else this would create more race conditions and make the already complex 2-repo release process for podman even more complex. 

As for a audit log, since we do have immutable releases here, we could just attach the record to the release? 

---

If the above sounds good, then I think the changes that need to be made to the design doc is 
1. Add script that verifies commit/pr approvals/tag is on a branch and not main
2. Add signature record as a release artifact
3. Add c/image changes to accept Fulcio/Rekor

> I think there's enough security there too that we don't have to worry about the workflow being maliciously edited - we have branch protection that prevents pushes and require pull requests for edits.

(Yes, with 1 required review.)

> I think I'd prefer to keep everything in the podman-machine-os repo. If this automation lived somewhere else this would create more race conditions and make the already complex 2-repo release process for podman even more complex.

I don’t feel too strongly about this, although it would be good to have a fairly wide consensus that we are fine with the level of protection. I suppose we could add branch protection rules “Require review from specific teams” or “Require review from Code Owners” for the workflow file.

> As for a audit log, since we do have immutable releases here, we could just attach the record to the release?

I think that would work fine, for the initial signing. We would ~lose the ability to re-sign an existing release, but per https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/pull/29973#discussion_r4361822889, it might be an option (strictly better?) to never re-sign, but to generate a new release from the same branch (assuming it is still buildable).

> If the above sounds good, then I think the changes that need to be made to the design doc is
> 
> 1. Add script that verifies commit/pr approvals/tag is on a branch and not main

To me “verifies the commit has the desired approvals / tag” is the important part; as for branch vs. main, I don’t think that matters strongly — _except_ that we must be able to sufficiently identify the trusted signing workflow in the OIDC token. But that would probably also be easier if we allowed the workflow from all branches, and not restricted it to specific branch names (because the current policy does not allow wildcards, and with PQC sigstore, wildcard matching might not even be an option).

> 2. Add signature record as a release artifact

(Recording what was signed, what is the signature, and all inputs to the “this is allowed to be signed” decision that the script verified, e.g. who approved it and the like.)

> 3. Add c/image changes to accept Fulcio/Rekor

This will need to figure out which of the exact items in the certificate, https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/blob/main/docs/oid-info.md , would be used to match. Compare https://github.com/containers/image/pull/2235#issuecomment-1874173317 , or ideally try generating a new example. Sadly it seems that the only workflow identifiers also include the branch name in a single item.

One way to adapt would be to design the workflow to always run from the same branch, if possible.

Another way to adapt would be to write code in c/image which strips the branch reference, and allow workflow-only matching — but it’s rather unclear whether that will work with the future PQC sigstore (https://github.com/sigstore/architecture-docs/blob/main/pqc-design.md#high-level-design says all contents will be hashed in the signature, and I don’t know whether the unhashed original will be shipped with the image). So if we go with the parsing+stripping approach, we might need to change things later, if this PQC sigstore design happens and after we decide to adopt it… taking on an amount of tech debt now.

> Another way to adapt would be to write code in c/image which strips the branch reference, and allow workflow-only matching — but it’s rather unclear whether that will work with the future PQC sigstore (https://github.com/sigstore/architecture-docs/blob/main/pqc-design.md#high-level-design says all contents will be hashed in the signature, and I don’t know whether the unhashed original will be shipped with the image).

Note to self, I have asked some experts about the plan.

I was pointed at https://github.com/kommendorkapten/protobuf-specs/blob/3629893dc3aa7808baca785953968153fb2065fd/protos/sigstore_bundle_v2.proto#L50-L54 , which suggests that the full string values _will_ be available, so we will be able to define logic based on parsing the values.

> Another way to adapt would be to write code in c/image which strips the branch reference, and allow workflow-only matching 

I think what we want instead of workflow matching is environment matching rather as the github environment allows us to set the approve rules if that is at all possible with sigstore
https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/manage-environments#creating-an-environment

I have not used them before but I think the OICD claim gets the environment value, i.e. cargo seem to recommend it  https://crates.io/docs/trusted-publishing
its also mentioned here for quay.io https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2026/07/22/push-images-to-quay-without-a-password
